name: La Llorona
description: The weeping woman who wanders the riverbanks at night, searching for her children

debut.title: Mexican legend
debut.era: colonial Mexico, from the 16th century onward

legend: The best-known version tells of a woman who, abandoned by the man she loved, drowned her children in a river and then drowned herself in grief. Now her spirit wanders near water at night in a white dress, crying for the children she lost. Some historians connect her to a weeping woman described among the omens of the Spanish conquest in the 16th-century Florentine Codex. Today the tale is told from Argentina to the American Southwest, often by parents who want children home before dark.

myths.claim: La Llorona's story is only told in Mexico.
myths.explanation: Versions are told across Latin America and in the southwestern United States.

myths.claim: Some trace her to a weeping woman in a 16th-century record of omens.
myths.explanation: The Florentine Codex describes a woman heard weeping at night among the omens before the conquest.

myths.claim: The legend is often used to keep children away from rivers at night.
myths.explanation: Generations of parents have warned that La Llorona might mistake a wandering child for her own.

powers: A wail that chills the blood
legacy: La Llorona (2019), Jayro Bustamante's acclaimed Guatemalan film
'La Llorona', a Mexican folk song still widely sung
facts: She wanders near rivers and lakes at night, crying for her lost children

hostIntro: If you hear crying down by the river tonight, don't go and look. Our guest has been searching the waterways for centuries.
